guidance.heading: Outlook
section: Geopolitical conditions have worsened since our last letter. The war in Iran has re-escalated and is now a broader Middle East conflict with attacks on Saudi Arabia and many other Gulf states. Energy and other commodity prices are rising again with reserve stockpiles nearly depleted. The resultant inflationary expectations drove fixed income markets to their worst quarterly performance in decades. U.S. 10-year Treasuries declined by nearly 8% in the quarter with yields at levels not seen in two decades. This despite the best efforts of the U.S. Treasury Department and Federal Reserve to convince markets that they could control inflation and force rates back down. Federal Reserve chairman Kevin Warsh delivered a hawkish speech in August. Then in September, the Federal Reserve raised rates 25 basis points more to preserve credibility than to have an economic impact. For his part, Treasury Secretary Bessent directed an intervention in the currency markets to prevent Japan from selling U.S. Treasuries to defend its currency. Next, Bessent raised the Treasury's commitment to buy back long dated issues. And finally, he declared “I am the house” in an effort to scare short-term traders into covering their short positions. None of these moves had more than a momentary impact on halting the rise in rates. Further, describing the Department of the Treasury as some kind of casino can hardly inspire confidence. We are reminded of the famous quote from the 1975 movie Jaws, “You are going to need a bigger boat.” Perhaps that’s why Secretary Bessent recently hired sound money advocate Judy Shelton as a Counselor to the Treasury Department. Shelton’s responsibilities are said to include “advising Bessent on currency policy, with a particular focus on evaluating financial conditions in China.” While Shelton was widely ridiculed by the Senate when President Trump nominated her for a Federal Reserve position during his first term, her views about backing long-term Treasuries with some linkage to gold may not be so far fetched today. A quick study of China will reveal its continued gold purchases and the lowest 10-year interest rates of any major economy other than Switzerland.

On the surface, equity markets seemed more resilient with major U.S. indices hitting all-time highs and the S&P 500 index itself closing the third quarter just 2% off its all-time high. But once again this was driven by a handful of mega-cap technology companies benefiting from the perceived limitless growth in artificial intelligence. The mean performance of all stocks in the S&P 500 was negative 21%. In the broader Russell 3000 index, 57% of the stocks were down more than 20%. It appears to us that the generals have gotten too far ahead of their troops.
